The summer of 1986 is now past and this issue blends some 
armchair reflections of summers gone by with some challenges for 
the summers yet to be. You can adventure into the past with the 
26,000 campers who participated in heritage programs this 
summer. There are summer ‘86 photos, program ideas and 
committee reports. Our personality profile highlights the life and 
work of Ted Yard. Ted’s wife and son (Shirley and Ted Jr.) 
provide the backbone of the profile but ‘T.Y.’s’ own writings fill 
out the scope of his impact on Canadian Camping. The 
International Camping Congress is now only a few months away. 
Look for detailed information on the Anne Nashman writing 
contest, and do some armchair writing of your own. Ted Yard 
would have been proud. 

DANS CETTE LIVRAISON 

L’ete 1986 est derriere nous. Cette livraison inclus un 
melange de reflections sur les etes passes ainsi que sur 
les defis que nous offrent ceux a venir. 

Joignez-vous aux 26,000 campeurs qui ont participe au 
programme “Heritage” cet ete. Vous y trouverez des 
photos de I’ete ‘86, des idees pour des programmes et des 
rapports de divers comites. 

Notre profil de personnalite evoque la vie et le travail de 
Ted Yard. Sa femme Shirley et son fils Ted nous 
fournissent I’information essentiel pour notre profil mais 
lesecritsdeT.Y. expriment par eux-memes. 

Nous ne sommes plus qu’a quelques mois du Congres 
International de Camping, vous trouverez plus d’infor- 
mation a ce sujet dans le concours de redaction d’Anne 
Nashman. Sortez vous plumes et ecrivez, Ted Yard en 
serait tier.

PRESIDENT’S 

MESSAGE 


At the beginning of October, the New Brunswick Camping 
Association hosted an Atlantic Regional Conference, in 
Moncton, for the Canadian Camping Association. This was 
combined with a workshop on the Camp Directors’ Curriculum 
for delegates from across Canada and a C.C.A. Board of 
Management meeting. A very active four days resulted from this 
gathering of camping people from across Canada, coming 
together for several purposes, but with a common goal — the 
development of camping. 

The New Brunswick Camping Association put forth all its 
efforts and provided lobster suppers, a sparkling conference 
featuring Michael Brandwein, and a celebration for C.C.A.*s 
fiftieth birthday. Rachelle Bordeleau the Conference chairman 
and Gillian Young who organized the birthday party ensured that 
we all left the Atlantic Region with many happy memories. The 
New Brunswick Camping Association is to be congratulated for 
great success in hosting this Regional Conference. 

Kelly Byrne, the Director of Camp Big Cove in Nova Scotia 
and the President of the Camping Association of Nova Scotia, 
has gathered a committed and enthusiastic group around her to 
provide direction and growth to their Association; and Frank 
O’Connor reports that, in Newfoundland, Association work is 
expanding very successfully. 

Camping certainly is alive and well in the Atlantic Provinces 
and I know that every delegate and representative from across 
Canada joins me in offering an accolade to the Atlantic Region 
Associations, and all their members. 


WHAT’S IN A NAME? 

The Art and Science of Camp names is a subject for detailed 
and prolonged study. The origins for some names are as simple as 
identifying the lake or mountain upon which the camp is located 
or the name of the founder or First director. Other names are 
complicated tongue twisting acronyms or they are native terms 
defying pronunciation by any but five year veterans of the camp 
itself. (Those campers and staff can even make it rhyme in the 
camp song). 

As its contribution to the language of camping the 
CANADIAN CAMPING MAGAZINE will send a crack team of 
investigative reporters into the archives of different camps across 
the country to deliver to its readership not only the correct 
pronunciation of the feature camp but the origin of its name as 
well. CANADIAN CAMPING MAGAZINE invites suggestions 
and data for future issues.

ILLAHEE NORTHWOODS CAMP 


Illahee was originally located on the shores of Lake Ontario 
near Cobourg and is now situated on Drag Lake in Haliburton. It 
is operated by the Family Service Association of Metropolitan 
Toronto. Fifty medically handicapped children (8 - 16) as well as 
twenty ‘regular’ teens attend camp at any one time. Activities 
include campcraft, canoeing, computers, archery, sailing, golf, 
tripping, swimming, tennis, and arts and crafts. 

The word “Northwoods” is a product of the change of site 
from Southern Ontario to the forests and lakes of Haliburton. 


The word “Illahee” comes from the Cree Indian language and 
it translates as ‘House by the Water*. The medical handicaps of 
Illahee campers would be very difficult in some other camp 
settings. These campers and all Illahee campers have come to love 
and appreciate their own special ‘House by the Water’.

D’une Cote A L’Autre

fQ 




f# ALBERTA 

With only 103 days between snow storms in 
many areas of the Province, our camping 
season has been brief but full and rewarding. 
The Senior Staff Workshop hosted by 
Pioneer Ranch was a great success — over 130 
delegates from 27 camps. The weekend was highlighted by the 
presence of John Jorgenson and Ken Whiteman. The two 
regional counsellor conferences were also successful events with a 
total of 150 counsellors attending. 

Spring expectations of a difficult summer because of the 
economy and Expo 86 proved to be true, but the impact was, in 
general, not nearly what was feared. Thanks to a generous grant 
from Recreation, Parks and Wildlife Foundation, our own 
Association contribution, and much hard work by Carson 
Herrick, we will have 27 delegates for the Camping Congress in 
Washington, D.C. 

Currently, preparations are now underway for our annual Fall 
Action Planning Weekend. In addition. Bob Sperling and Mike 
Walters attended the Camping Training Workshop in New 
Brunswick for the new Curriculum for Camp Directors developed 
by C.C.A.

QUEBEC 

Y We had been dreaming since quite a while 

VA# about updating the classification of archives 
7WVv at the Association! Well, in April, Employ¬ 
ee yQ\ ment and Immigration Canada granted 

/ A \ A.C.Q. a project which allowed us to have a 
team of three persons who worked all summer 
at reclassifying all archives and all camp dossiers of the 
Association. 

The new classification system derived for the camp dossiers was 
of great help to the three accreditation consultants who visited a 
total of 76 camps during the summer. Leo Venditti, Yves Legault 
and Louis Jean did all visits; four of the visits were for new- 
members. 

Promotion also got a boost during the summer, Jean-Marc 
Amyot of the audio-visual services at R.L.Q. visited, camera in 
hand, a few of our camps and came back with some 400 slides. A 
slide show will be completed during the fall. Three copies of the 
show will be produced and the sound cassette will be available in 
both languages. 

You have already received copy of a pamphlet produced in 
collaboration with the M.L.C.P. to promote outdoor education 
classes. This pamphlet was printed in 50,000 French copies and 
8,000 English copies and was distributed, in September, to all 
school principals and consultants of the Province. 

A similar pamphlet will be published later this year under the 
theme: “Employment in a Summer Camp”. The pamphlet will 
be intended to promote employment in summer camps and to 
provide interested youth with the basic information. 

ATLANTIC REGIONAL NEWS 

by Ian Fowler — C.C.A./A.C.C. Vice-President 
(Atlantic Region) 

The summer of 1986 will be remembered in many different 
ways by each Atlantic Region Camp. In general, all camps 
enjoyed successful summers with increases in the number of 
children attending camp reported throughout the region. Camp 
participation in the C.C.A.’s 50th Anniversary celebrations 
through the Adventure Into The Past Program was limited. 
However, those participating found the program to be enjoyable. 
As well, a tip of the hat goes to ATV and the Halifax YMCA who 
co-operated in a “Consumer Watch” feature on preparing your 
child for camp, and selecting a children’s camp. Aired throughout 
Atlantic Canada, this was a very positive promotion for youth 
camping. 

Finally, the summer was busy preparing for the 1st Atlantic 
Region Conference which was held in Moncton October 4-6. 

NOVA SCOTIA 

Summer camps enjoyed a successful 
summer in Nova Scotia with all camps 
n n reporting a good enrollment. Through the 

efforts of a Job-Creation Grant, we 
were aWe t0 hire Joanne Jefferson who 


visited several camps and assisted in the promotion of C.A.N.S. 
An executive meeting in mid-August put together the require¬ 
ments for a Planning Seminar to be held in Halifax, October 
17th - 18th which we feel will provide new direction and 
momentum for the Camping Association of Nova Scotia. 

NEW BRUNSWICK 

A On October 1st to 3rd, 1986 the New 
Brunswick Camping Association held the first 
Atlantic Regional Conference “A Half 
Century of Service and Growth”. This 
title was to acknowledge the Canadian Camping Association’s 
fiftieth anniversary. Seventy-five delegates attended this very 
successful event, which was highlighted by the leadership of 
Michael Brandwein, a lawyer and communication expert from 
Chicago. 

NOUVEAU BRUNSWICK 

▲ Du 1 ®r au 3 oct., 1986,1’Association des 

Camps du Nouveau-Brunswick a 6te 
i’hote de la premiere conference 
Regionale de PAtlantique “Un demi- 
sifecle de service et de croissance”. Ce 
th6me voulait soulign6 le 50© Anniversaire de I’A.C.C. 
Soixante-quinze detegues ont assiste & cet 6v6nement

un avocat et expert en communication de Chicago. 

The New Brunswick Camping Association and its camp 
members enjoyed an active and successful summer. Although the 
weather was inclement most camps reported a solid increase in 
attendance. The association’s zone reps were busy throughout the 
summer making camp visitations, while the Training Committee 
hosted two successful spring workshops. The association looks 
forward to its upcoming meeting at which time the Association’s 
3 -year plan will be reviewed and extended.

NEWFOUNDLAND 
The 1986 summer may well be remem- 

I bered as the summer that never happened 

— rr "~ in Newfoundland, yet despite generally 
cooler and overcast weather camping was 
not dampened in the least. All the camps in the province, most of 
which are church or agency camps, functioned to normal capacity 
and generally reported a good year. The Newfoundland and 
Labrador Camping Association has resumed its fall meeting series 
and is planning for a winter camp leadership and skills workshop 
in early January. 

An updated Provincial Camp Directory will soon be published 
and a fall newsletter is imminent. Included in the winter season's 
plans is to send six delegates to the International Camping 
Conference in Washington next March, and to host a leader 
training seminar in conjunction with a Spring Conference and 
Workshop in April, to which C.C.A. president Janet Adamson is 
to be invited. 

Frank O’Connor, President, N.L.C.A.

stuff that history is made of”.

The current task for the committee has 
been to work with a printer to complete 
the publication of the Curriculum for 
Camp Directors. The process involved a 
submission to Fitness Canada to assist in 
the publication of the English and French 
versions. A tendering process was initiated 
to Find the printer. Proofs were approved 
by Fitness Canada and now it is the 
committee’s intention to have the publi¬ 
cation in circulation before the end of 
October. The workshop in Moncton was 
to have as its focus for one day, the 
Curriculum —its use, its promotion and 
benefits provincially and nationally to the 
camping and outdoor community. It will 
be in a binder, with an attractive graphics 
on the cover and the contents also include 
an extensive bibliography. 

Plans for the future include continued 
research on the bibliography but a great 
amount of committee time will be given to 
assisting each province with whatever 
results and actions are forth-coming from 
the meeting in Moncton. 

D. Walter, 
Chairman

A fund raising drive led by Jack Pearse

community across Canada. Fund raising 
will continue as this concept is developed 
and expanded by the Fund Raising 
Committee.

“Dave Sands: Liaison to 1987 International 
Camping Congress” 

National Conferences and 
Workshops Committee 

by Glenn Bamed 

Workshops usually have two sides to 
their make-up. One side is the social 
activity that builds the group and 
strengthens their commitment towards the 
results of the workshop. The other facet is 
the actual work and the results that come 
out during the event. As members of the 
1986 National Workshop gathered in 
Moncton, New Brunswick, on 
Wednesday, October the first, it indeed 
looked like it was going to be a super 
workshop. Wednesday evening began 
with delegates from each Provincial 
Association introducing themselves and 
explaining a little about their connection 
with Canadian Camping. Bob Latimer, a 
trainer from the National Training 
Institute, led us through the first two days 
of our workshop. The purpose and 
direction for the workshop was briefly 
outlined by Bob and the group broke for 
free time while we began to meld into a 
cohesive group. 

Day two — On Thursday, we began to 
look at the curriculum for Camp 
Directors’ development. Dorothy Walter 
and her Committee put together an 


The summer was not the most 
favourable for our projects since we had a 
very busy season. 

We have a new committee member in 
Michel Gratton of Hearst, Ontario. We 
thus have two “out-of-Quebec” 
members which should help promote the 
reality of French in the camping world. 


6 




excellent tool to educate Canadian Camp 
Directors. At the workshop, it was our 
task to decide the best method for using 
the tool and taking it back to each 
Province. The group struggled in terms of 
trying to discover the document and what 
it actually was, the history behind it, and 
how it was intended to be used. We 
developed three sample prototype work¬ 
shops which could be used by Provincial 
Camping Associations to educate their 
Camp Directors. 

Day three — On Friday, we started the 
second facet of our workshop by looking 
at volunteer Board member development. 
The purpose of this part of the workshop 
was to assist delegates in the continuing 
process of developing their Provincial 
Boards and individual members. The 
morning sessions began by examining the 
planning process and working through 
several exercises of developing plans, 
looking at long-range and strategic 
planning, planning-by-objective steps, 
and generally the nature of planning with 
errors and pitfalls. After a terrific break 
for lunch outside the hotel complex, we 
studied various aspects of volunteerism. 
Upon examining the rationale and values 
of volunteerism, we looked more closely 
at recruitment in terms of the hows and 
whys of attaining the appropriate and 
committed volunteers. This was the end of 
Bob Latimer’s time with us, so he thanked 
us and we thanked him for our mutual 
efforts in the workshop. 

On the evening of Friday, we attended 
the opening of the First Regional 
Conference to be held in Eastern Canada. 
The kickoff began with an address by 
Jocelyn Palm who provided a thought- 
provoking informative talk using Charlie 
Brown and others to explore the role of 
Camp, campers and staff. A super way to 
begin a super Conference. 

Day four — Saturday was a tremen¬ 
dous hit as the delegates attended Michael 
Brandwein’s sessions at the Regional 
Conference. The purpose was not only to 
take back the information and meat from 
Michael’s sessions, but also to examine his 
style and techniques of delivery of his 
various sessions. Michael is a very 
dynamic and positive trainer who 
captures the interest and attention of 
every person in the room and he was an 
excellent role model for all trainers. The 
evening was topped off with a 50th 
Birthday Party for the Canadian Camping 
Association. To celebrate our 
Anniversary, the New Brunswick 
Camping Association provided cake, 
balloons, fun and games for everyone. A 
very nice way to end a long and enjoyable 
day at a Conference. 

Day five — On Sunday, the delegates 
from the Canadian Camping Association 
National Workshop regrouped once more 
to finish our workshop. We began with an 
overview of the first four days and how 


and why the various items occurred. Next, 
we evaluated Michael Brandwein’s 
sessions in terms of the methods and styles 
he used to see which would be appro¬ 
priate or could be used in a “back-home” 
setting. The trainers sensed the power 
Michael had by being positive and 
dynamic and using his own “Ten 
Commandments in Communication” in 
terms of his training style. Our next step 
was to examine the Board development 
sessions in terms of planning and 
volunteerism. Various delegates shared 
how they were going to make use of this 
information and how they would pass it 
on using events and activities that were 
already happening back in their 
Provinces. This sharing of ideas and 
suggestions enhanced the learning that 
took place and also provided many new 
ideas for the delegates to utilize at home. 

Then, we tackled the curriculum for 
Camp Directors. A statement was made 
about the documentation that would be 
sent to all the delegates within six weeks of 
the workshop. These would include the 
three sample prototype workshops as well 
as supporting material for these 
workshops; a shopping list of other 
possible uses of the curriculum which 
could be considered by the Provincial 
Associations; a contact sheet for 
networking between the delegates; and 
other pieces of information as requested 
by the delegates. Janet Adamson shared a 
proposed action plan which took the 
delegates through a step-by-step process 
beginning with the final day of the 
Conference, through the initial steps of 
how to work through their Boards and 
their Education or Training Committees 
to a point of putting on the first workshop 
in their Province and begin to train Camp 
Directors using the curriculum as designed 
by the Professional Development 
Committee. 

A suggestion was quickly picked up to 
ask the Executive of CCA to produce a 
certificate to acknowledge a Camp 
Director’s completion of, or attendance 
at, training for the Camp Director’s 
personal development. 

This brought us close to the conclusion 
of the workshop with the usual 
evaluations and with one unique twist. A 
contract was produced which the dele¬ 
gates were asked to sign along with the 
President of CCA. The contract basically 
formed a commitment on behalf of the 
delegates and of CCA. By signing the 
contract, the delegates agreed to take the 
information of the workshop back to the 
Provinces and continue with Board 
development and Camp Directors’ 
development. The CCA President agreed 
to do a follow-up with the delegates, to 
provide the documentation from this 
workshop, to provide input and resources 
as requested for both the Board develop¬ 
ment and the Camp Directors’ 


development, and finally, a commitment 
from herself to the intent of the work¬ 
shop. The contracts included specific 
dates for the delegates to complete the 
first steps of getting “the ball rolling in 
their Provinces”. There were also dates 
set for follow-up to be done by the 
President of CCA. 

Many many people have to be 
thanked for the success of this National 
Workshop. To mention a few, I would 
have to include Johnny Comfort, 
McSweeny’s Bar and Grill, Janet 
Adamson — President of CCA, Dorothy 
Walter — Chairman of the Professional 
Development Committee, Ian 
Fowler — Vice President of the CCA, 
Rochelle Bordeleau — Chairman of the 
Regional Conference and all the members 
of her Committee who helped to make our 
workshop run smoothly. A final “thank 
you” to all the delegates from the 
Provinces, the Provinces who assisted 
them and to the Board members of CCA 
who attended part of our workshop. It is 
the calibre of the people the Provinces 
sent that will keep CCA strong and 
growing. The results of this workshop will 
be seen in every Province across Canada. 
If you wish to get more information on 
the Board development or on the 
curriculum for Camp Directors, I urge 
you to contact the representative from 
your Province. 

In conclusion, I would have to say that 
the delegates left the Canadian National 
Workshop as a joint body to further the 
interests of Canadian Camping. To sum it 
up with one quotation, I would use the 
words from the song which ended our 
vesper service on Sunday morning: “The 
road that we are travelling is long ‘till 
journey’s end; we share one destination 
so walk with me, my friend”.

Cet article nous donne les grandes legnes d’un programme des plus 
interessant qui se developpe au Camps Gay Venture. 

Grace a une cabane en bois sur place, les campeurs ont I’occasion de se 
familiariser avec leur heritage passe. Pieces de musee, d’arts et archives sont 
a leur disposition. 

Several years ago we started a Pioneer Craft Program at GayVenture that has grown 
into an activity centre called at our camp “The Log Cabin” but which really should be 
named the “Pioneer Museum and Activity Program”. 

This activity has proven to be very successful and I am going to detail very briefly 
the components. 

PHYSICAL SITE — in the woods removed from other activity areas 

— a log cabin, either moved from another site, or constructed 
from local logs. The building can be of a very simple design 

— the cabin is set up with pioneer artifacts (listed below), dis¬ 
played and set up for use 

— one section is furnished as a pioneer kitchen with a wood 
stove used for cooking 

— pioneer costumes (aprons and bonnets) are available for 
campers to wear for some activities. 

The program has four components — Pioneer Museum, Pioneer Craft Activities, 
Associated Activities, and a Camp Archival Collection. 

Pioneer Museum — collect and display with labels: candle snuffers, pioneer 
tools, farm implements, butter churn, pioneer kitchen 
implements, lanterns, furniture, pumps, wagon wheels 

— the collection grows as people donate items 

— we have slowly added more up-to-date items that today’s 
campers have never seen in use, such as, an old lawn mower, 
the original camp pump, meat grinders — the list can be 
endless. 


Pioneer Craft Activities — soap making, candle making, cooking (mainly muffins 

and buns, jams from berries picked in July), rug weaving, 
apple dolls, reed weaving, nature dyeing, quilting, 
Christmas decorations from pine cones and nuts, 
pioneer three-legged stools, paper making, spinning 
wool, embroidery 

— there are many resources from which to secure recipes 
and activity ideas, in libraries and at local pioneer 

villages. Continued on Page 9 






The Earth Speaks, Acclimatization Ex¬ 
periences Institute, 184 p., 1983.

A PIONEER CENTRE (cont’d from page 8) 
— visits to local museums, Pioneer Days including corn 
roasts, cabin group overnights in “the Log Cabin”, 
pancake breakfasts for a cabin group in “the Log 
Cabin”, theme activities based on living history in which 
campers are involved in a rotation from station to 
station at which pioneer life scenes are set up and 
demonstrated, such as “the school teacher”.

Les Lignes 



Camp Archival Collection — a collection of old camp photos, crests, brochures, 

letters, manuals 

— these are displayed in one area of the cabin for 
campers to browse through 

— again this collection grows as former campers and 
staff donate items. 

This is a very brief description of a “Pioneer Centre”. It is an activity that grows 
from small beginnings. Each component can be developed a great deal and grows each 
year. A Pioneer Centre adds a richness to camp life and becomes a centre that campers 
and staff enjoy visiting as part of their daily life at camp. For instance, we often have 
hot chocolate on the stove in the cabin and campers drop in on their way home from 
swimming, and look for a picture of their mother in the photo collection. 

Once you start this activity you will find that the resources and ideas available to 
expand it are endless and very varied depending on your geographical location. I would 
imagine that in the Maritimes the history of fishing could be used and in areas of Indian 
activity, this could be included. I don’t know if any camps have archeological digs but 
there are experts who probably would love to use an area of your camp for one. 


A “Pioneer Centre”, why not try it?

PERSONALITY PROFILE 


Le Profil De Personnalite 


W. E. (Ted) Yard i- 

(1919 - 1983) | 

Ted Yard was the Director of the 
Toronto Y.M.C.A. Camp Pine Crest 
from 1946 - 1963 and his own private 
independent Camp Hollyburn from 
1968 - 1982. In the intervening years, he ^ 

and Alex “Sass” Peepre conducted a 
wilderness canoe-tripping program for 
the Sault Ste. Marie Family Y.M.C.A., 
when Ted was General Secretary of that 
Association. 

Ted was President of the Canadian ^ 

Camping Association from 1953 - 1955 
and, during that time, he and his family 
drove across Canada visiting each 
Provincial Camping Association and 
many Camps along the way. 

He was President of the Ontario 
Camping Association from 1950 - 1952 

and had a second tour of duty with _ 

the O.C.A. Board as Treasurer from 
1971 - 74. CANADIAN CAMPING 
MAGAZINE conducted this interview 
with Ted’s wife, Shirley, and their son, 

Ted, who along with his wife, Darlene, 
directs Camp Hollyburn. 


INTERVIEW WITH SHIRLEY YARD 
AND TED YARD JR. 

CANADIAN CAMPING: Did Ted always know he wanted a 
career in camping? 

SHIRLEY YARD: I don’t think so because he started out 
working with young people at a very early age himself. 
Actually, he started working with young people through 
boxing. 

CC: Where was that, Shirley? 

SY: In Vancouver. Of course, I didn’t know Ted then, so I have 
to reach back and pull out little bits of information he may 
have told me along the way. I think he started out working 
with inner-city boys .... gangs .... if you would like to 
call them that.... who during the war needed someone to 
give them direction. Through working with these boys, the 
“Y” asked him if he would like to bring this program into 
the “Y”. 

CC: So, his work with youth started outside the YMCA. 

SY: I think so, to do with his boxing, because he was a golden 
glove boxer himself and because he was able to use the 
facilities at the “Y”. The YMCA said to him at one point, 
“If you will work for us, we will send you to University.” 
It was then that he started a group called the Triple C, 
which meant City Camp Counsellors — this, I believe, 
was around 1941 - 42, somewhere in there. 

CC: And that was under the auspices of the YMCA in 
Vancouver. 

SY: Well, these were boys who were in these gangs, who were 
programmed through the “Y” but were not in the “Y” 
necessarily. He also started a Boys* Town. These were the 
same young boys who came in and met there once a week. 
Through these groups, he got his interest in camping be¬ 
cause he had ... the first winter camp ... I don’t know if 


iatj, 


W. E. (Ted) Yard 
(1919-1983) 

Ted Yard a ete le dlrecteur du Camp 
Pine Crest du YMCA de Toronto de 
1946 -1963, et de son propre camp, le 
Camp Hollyburn, de 1968 - 1982. Dans 
I’intermediaire, il a dirige avec I’aide 
d’Alex “Sass” Peepre un programme 
d’explorations en canot pour le YMCA 
familial de Sault Ste-Marie. II etait 
alors le secretaire general de cette 
association. 

Ted tut president de I’A.C.C. de 
1953-1955 et pendant ce temps il a 
traverse avec sa famille tout le 
Canada, visitant chaque association 
provenciale de camping en plus de 
plusieurs Camps. 

II a ete le president de O.C.A. de 
1950 - 52 et pour son deuxieme sejour 
avec O.C.A. il tut membre du Conseil 
du Tresorde 1971 -74. 

Le magazine de Camping Canadien 
a realise cet interview avec Shirley, sa 
femme et Ted, son fils qui, avec sa 
femme Darlene, dirige maintenant le 
Camp Hollyburn. 


it was the first the “Y” ever had, but it was called Skyline 
Boys’ Camp. It was with boys from the different gangs . . . 
they called them gangs, too. 

CC: In West Vanvouver or ....? 

SY: All over Vancouver. 

TED YARD JR.: It began in the west end, right down in that 
very dense part of town. I read some clippings in Dad’s 
scrap book that showed this to be the beginning of the 
whole Lower Mainland “Y” . . . they were training 
leaders. The article mentioned they couldn’t train leaders 
fast enough for this new program that started in the west 
end for the “gang” kind of thing. So, that is where it 
all began. 

CC: It wasn’t camping, but he called the group “City Camp 
Counsellors”. 

SY: Yes, because one of their objectives was to take the boys 
out of the city into a camp situation and these gangs . . . 
it worked so well. . . having the gangs have their own little 
association ... it worked so well as Ted says, “They had 
to keep training new leaders because so many of them 
wanted to be in on this”. 

TY: Well, all of the other YMCA’s in the Lower Mainland 
wanted to start similar programs. 

SY: As a matter of fact, some of the Triple C er’s, many years 
later, worked with Ted at Camp Pine Crest. 

CC: So, the YMCA in Vancouver hired Ted full time and he 
went to the University of British Columbia at the same 
time... 

SY: For about 3 years, because it was around 1945 when he got 
his degree in order to qualify as a YMCA Secretary. 

CC: Were there people in Vancouver who influenced him in 
those early years? 


10 






11 






In those days if a YMCA camp had any profit, it often went 
back into the City Branch to maintain that part of the 
operation but, with Ted, I guess he was able to use all of 
his budget, was he? 

Well, eventually. Originally when Ted went there, the 
Camp was subsidized because it had just gone through the 
war years and things were not in good shape either 
financially or physically. As the years went along, it 
became apparent that this could be a self-supporting 
Branch. It paid all the salaries, it re-built ... at that time 
when Ted was there the whole camp was re-built, literally 
and figuratively ... all paid out of the operation. Now, I 
know there were little mortgages along the way but they 
were dispensed with in due course. 

In those eighteen years at Camp Pine Crest, there were 
some really important things that happened in YMCA 
Camping because of the things Ted was doing, like year- 
round camping and having Pine Crest as a Branch of the 
Toronto YMCA. What else went on, then? 

You mean like the re-building of the whole Camp? That 
was done over a number of years, of course, but it was a 
vast project and I think this is one reason why Ted stayed 
in camping at Pine Crest for so long, because he had a goal. 
He hadn’t finished doing all the things he wanted to do to 
build Pine Crest up to what it was when he left, both 
financially independent and physically refurbished 
completely and . .. 




“The 'new' winter lodge at Camp Pine Crest and some of the earliest 

winter camping in Canada** 

CC: Have you thought of something, Ted? 

TY: Yes, it wasn’t only a physical re-building, or even the 
financial management, but it was putting his own personal 
stamp on the place, too, and establishing his own leader¬ 
ship there. I know he related to me what a difficult time it 
was when he first arrived there. He inherited the staff that 
was already at Pine Crest for that summer and I guess it was 
a pretty tough situation because they didn’t know who he 
was and vice-versa. There was no question about it, he had 
to establish the kind of philosophy of sticking to principles, 
I guess, and making his staff also live by them. That was 
really starting after the first year, establishing his leader¬ 
ship in that way. After that when he was able to hire his 
own staff, it changed. It was a little easier, but those first 
few years were particularly difficult, from that standpoint, 
not just from re-building but from establishing his 
leadership. 

CC: Well if he hadn’t done that, he wouldn’t have been able to 
live with himself, to start with, but it would have been 
impossible then for Camp Pine Crest to be the kind of 
Camp Ted Yard knew he wanted it to be. 


TY: I think it was all part of putting his own principles and 
ideals on the line. The Camp had to be that and the people 
working there had to do that. This carried on throughout 
the 18 years he was at Pine Crest. He was very much his 
own ... it was a very important part of his imprint on the 
place. 

CC: People in camping, in general, looked to Ted as the voice 
of YMCA camping in the country and there were things 
he did, both through the Camping Committee of the 
YMCA National Council and through his time at Pine 
Crest, that made an impact on camping. Can you recall 
any of those things? 

SY: Ted had very strong feelings about certain ways or 
directions the Camping Association should go and he was 
not the kind of person who held back on anything like this. 
He said that, if he didn’t agree with something, he would 
come right out and say so. It is not exactly how you win 
friends and influence people. You could influence people, 
but you might lose your friends. Occasionally, I think this 
is what would happen and then, in the long run, it would 
be for the betterment of everybody . . . both the Associ¬ 
ation and the camping movement. 

CC: He felt so strongly about things and he would say it right 
from the shoulder the way it was. At the time, it was hard 
to swallow but, in retrospect, we remember all the 
enormous contributions he made and how important they 
really were to camping. 

SY: Well, I think so too. Ted believed that he couldn’t sit back 
and not speak out. Usually, it turned out that most people 
would agree with him. He was not always right. . . nobody 
ever is; but in some instances his ideals and principles 
were very strong and this got him into hot water. I think 
most people valued this about him. There was one time 
when he was President of the Canadian Camping Associ¬ 
ation and he decided he would like to visit every Camping 
Association across the country and at that point I believe 
we had two children. 

CC: Judy and Jack. 

SY: Yes, Judy and Jack ... so, for our holidays we decided we 
would do a cross-country trip in the car with these two 
little kids. He had arranged ahead of time and he visited 
and spoke to every Association going west from Ontario. 
We didn’t go east. I don’t know whether there were 
Associations at that time in the east. (Ed’s note: At that 
time, the Quebec Camping Association was the only 
Provincial Association east of Ontario). We went west 
and I can remember sometimes I would not be able ... I 
would be in a motel with these two little kids and Ted 
would be busy speaking somewhere and then the next 
thing we knew we would roar onto the next place. It was a 
wonderful thing, actually, because people knew at these 
Associations that Ted was the leader in the Canadian 
Camping Association. A lot of them needed help along 
the way in those early days because it was a new thing, 
wasn’t it? 

CC: The really important thing you did and Ted did, as 
President, was to make that trip and to have everybody 
across the country feel they were an integral part of a 
nationwide movement. Wow! 

SY: And that it wasn’t just Ontario ... 

CC: You know, shortly after that, people recognized there were 
camping people everywhere across the country who could 
lead the National Association because, up until that time, 
the President of the Canadian Camping Association was 
either from Quebec or from Ontario (and even more 
specifically from Montreal or Toronto) and, shortly after 
you made your cross-Canada trip, it began that Presidents 
and Executives and Boards of the Canadian Camping 


12 




Association were provincially-located. It was a monu¬ 
mental thing you did and it must have been an enormous 
sacrifice... 

SY: Well, not really, I mean when you’re at that stage you 
don’t mind doing those things. Now, when I look back, I 
wonder how on earth we ever did it but not when you’re 
young and interested in what you’re doing and you are 
living a life of camping. Another thing that Ted did, I don’t 
know what year it was, was a survey on YMCA Camp 
Stephens for Don Phelan. They re-constructed the whole 
Camp according to his survey. That would be in the sixties 
because Don Phelan went to Winnipeg YMCA in 1962, 
the year before we went to Sault Ste. Marie. 

CC: In 1959 when he was doing his Masters program at George 
Williams College in Chicago, he put together a Camp 
Director’s Calendar month by month throughout the 
year that many, many people still use. 

SY: Yes, that was a big contribution for him to have done 
that... I didn't know about that... I mean I knew he did 
something but I didn’t realize it was that significant... 

CC: Oh boy! As a matter of fact, it is still in use . . . the Ted 
Yard Camp Director’s Calendar. Do you want to mention 
other things he did for the Y? 

SY: There was a project of the Boys’ Work Committee of the 
National Council YMCA. It is a survey of costs and 
factors in Canadian YMCA Camps. This is probably what 
he did his thesis on when he completed his Master’s 
degree at George Williams College in 1958/59. 

CC: During those eighteen years at Camp Pine Crest, can you 
recall the names of any people that might have influenced 
him even more in his professional career... 

SY: Definitely, Ken Lemon would be one. He was a Committee 
Chairman in 1946,1 think, when Ted first came from the 
West. Ken has been an influence and still is an influence in 
all that the Yard family did. He was one person who 
definitely helped Ted in more ways than one. Sometimes 
when he needed support, particularly in his decisions to 
do with his direction in camping .... another is Sass 
Peepre. He came to Canada and to Camp Pine Crest in 
1950. He could not speak English and, almost every day, 
Ted took an hour or so to help him learn English. Their 
friendship grew from that and from their common interest 
in the out-of-doors and skiing, woodcraft, teaching young 
people how to live and love the out-of-doors . . . and 
also in introducing orienteering to North America ... we 
have a memorial orienteering course at Hollybum named 
for Sass and this is where he will go on forever. 

CC: At one time, the American Army had Sass as their expert 
on Orienteering and particularly as it related to cross¬ 
country skiing... orienteering on skis. 

SY: Well, if it hadn’t been for Sass, orienteering would have 
come to North America eventually, I am sure, but he was 
the one who introduced it back in the late 50’s. 

CC: And then the outdoor-related courses that Sass taught at 
the University of Guelph were strongly influenced by Ted 
because of Sass’ early association. 

SY: I would say that Sass helped Ted to maintain his interest in 
the out-of-doors and to develop his interest along 
different lines. 

TY: There was a reinforcement there for Dad, too. Sass shared 
many of the same kind of values and perhaps you might 
go as far as saying some of his inflexible ideals about 
things. I think they both shared a lot of those things. 

SY: They were both very strong people. 

CC: Who, besides me and many other grateful former YMCA 
Camp Directors, did Ted influence during those years? 


SY: Well, I would certainly say he influenced a great many 
young people because, especially since Ted has been gone, 
they have made a point of telling me this; there is one 
person in particular who is still associated with Hollybum 
and his name is John Hawkins. Quite openly he said “If 
it hadn’t been for Ted, I wouldn’t be the person I am 
today, physically or mentally’’. But there are many people 
like that. It would be hard to name them all, to rhyme 
it all off because... 

CC: There are some that became Camp Directors . . . like Kirk 
Wipper for example... 

SY: When Kirk first came to Pine Crest I don’t think many 
people know that he couldn’t paddle a canoe at all. He 
and Ted used to go out and paddle canoes for hours on 
end. I felt that maybe Ted influenced Kirk in his love of 
canoes ... I don’t know that he did in developing his 
Kanawa Museum but I do know that Pine Crest was where 
Kirk first learned to paddle a canoe. 

CC: Well, canoes and canoeing became a passion with Kirk 
to the point where his is now recognized as one of the 
experts in the world. 

SY: Oh, I know someone else who might be interesting to tell 
you about is John Waadland ... he teaches at Trent 
University. I am not sure what he teaches but he has a 
doctorate now and he got his ... he wrote his thesis on 
Ernest Thompson Seton because of Ted. Ted had a 
collection of Seton’s books and it was while at Pine Crest, 
as a counsellor, that he interested John in Ernest 
Thompson Seton and loaned him a lot of these books. 
Afterwards, he sent this thesis to Ted and at the frontJohn 
acknowledged Ted which I thought was really wonderful. 
It made Ted feel pretty proud. 

CC: Was there any Indian Council emphasis at Pine Crest. . . 
because of Ted’s love for Ernest Thompson Seton’s 
writing? 

SY: Only a Council fire once a week, if it was even that. Ted 
did not... we don’t do that at Hollybum either ... we 
only have it once in the year ... an actual Indian theme, 
because for some reason I think Ted . • . not that people 
don’t respect the Indian . . . but he felt that we should not 
make a big thing out of Indian Lore by imitating them but 
by celebrating with them. This was a different sort of 
concept. . . . that’s the feeling I always got . . . that he 
didn’t want to play up an Indian theme as such. 

TY: Even when we do our Indian Councils now, we are 
actually teaching them what the ceremony is because it is a 
very serious thing we do. From what I remember of Pine 
Crest, it was very much like that and in many of the 
letters we receive from former Pine Cresters, their most 
vivid memory is of Dad coming across in a canoe standing 
up being paddled by his Medicine Man coming to the 
Council Ring. It was a very moving experience for virtually 
every Pine Crester who took part in it because it was 
handled in that sort of way. 

SY: There were only three campfires for the three periods. And 
my children didn’t even know for a long time that their 
father was the Chief. 

CC: He was in costume... 

SY: Oh yes, and nobody knew. 

CC: But he had this respect for Ernest Thompson Seton and it 
must have been because of his knowledge and sharing his 
knowledge of Indian culture and Ceremony... 

SY: It was a real respect for it; there was no imitating, it was 
more teaching this ceremonial part of it. I think Ted felt 
quite strongly about that and there again was another 
reason why we didn’t call our Camp an Indian name. Of 
course, the main reason we called it “Hollybum” was the 
happy memory of Hollybum Ridge on the west coast. 


13 





CC: We have been interweaving Pine Crest and Hollyburn 
throughout this interview and we should get to Hollyburn 
soon. Meanwhile, the years between the finish of Pine 
Crest and the start of Hollyburn .. . let’s talk about that a 
little bit . . . his stint with the YMCA at Sault St. Marie 
was from... 

SY: 1963 to 1967. In 1963, Ted felt he had achieved the goals 
he had set for himself at Pine Crest. It was time to make a 
change and grow in a different way. Mind you, I should 
tell you that all through these years, from the time I knew 
Ted which was ‘46, we had always had a dream of starting 
or finding our own Camp. We had looked virtually from 
the east coast to the west coast and had never found the 
perfect site so, with going to Sault St. Marie, we thought 
“Well, we have been looking for twenty years. I guess we 
will never find it, so we will make our home in Sault St. 
Marie”. During that 3Vi years, Ted couldn’t keep out of 
camping and, along with Sass Peepre, he started the first 
young people’s canoe-trip in Sault St. Marie. There had 
been some camping going on there. It was day camping 
mostly at a place called Pawating. Because Sault St. Marie 
was already in the wilderness, there was not really that 
much need for establishing any kind of resident Camp. 
Anybody who went to Camp, as we know a resident Camp, 
usually went to John Island which is associated with the 
Sudbury YMCA. But back to Sass and Ted taking the first 
canoe trip. It really blossomed from there and was so 
successful that I understand after we left they went into a 
lot of extended canoe-tripping and they even bought a van. 
We had been 3 Vi years in Sault St. Marie and Ted, I guess, 
began to feel a little restless. We hadn’t been in camping 
and... 

TY: ... maybe we should mention a little bit about the new Y 
there before we move on... 

SY: ... he went up there specifically to build... or to supervise 
the building of a new Family YMCA. It was a different 
kind of life for Ted in that he was in a more executive 
position rather than an outdoor Camp man. 

CC: When was the new Y built... 

SY: It was built in 1964. The old Y was still there. They had to 
go out on a second campaign because there wasn’t enough 
money. Then, the old Y was demolished and the new Y 
built. I remember Lester Pearson came and laid the corner 
stone which was very exciting and there also was a coming 
together of the various religious groups in Sault St. Marie. 
It is almost 50 - 50 Roman Catholic and Protestant and, at 
that point, there was not much ecumenism going on, but 
the Y seemed to bring all those groups together. It was 
the facility for the people; there was no other swimming 
pool; there weren’t many recreational buddings as such; 
the family could participate as a group. It was the first 
Family Y in Canada. 

CC: During that V/i years, were you still hunting for your 
dream place? 

SY: Yes, as a matter of fact, it was the first time in Ted’s and 
my life together that we had not had any place to Camp. So 
what did we do but buy some property near Parry Sound, 
on an island, and our 3-week holiday was spent cutting 
down trees and making logs, clearing off logs . . . what do 
you call it. . . stripping logs, skinning logs and building a 
log cabin for our own little Camp. 

CC: Now, was that near the site of Hollyburn... 

SY: Well, by golly, it was 2 stone throws away ... it really was, 
it was Parry Sound and you know where we are in Rosseau. 

CC: So you ... 

SY: Do you want me to get into how we moved... 


CC: Sure . . . This must have been really hard at first... for 
Ted to end his long and distinguished career in the 
YMCA.... 

SY: Yes, but... 

CC: And then start at that stage in his life to build a Camp. 

SY: Actually Ted was starting to . . . just heard that the 
Community Colleges were starting up and he decided that 
maybe he would go and see if there was anything he could 
do related to camping with the Colleges. And the funny 
thing was that, right about the same time, somebody told 
him to take a look at this place on Lake Rosseau on his 
way down to Toronto. He had a clipping from the Globe 
and Mail with an advertisement that mentioned this 
property near Rosseau and he thought, well, that’s right on 
the way, so he took this fellow with him, Ted, because it 
was your birthday or something... 

TY: But it was fate too... 

CC: You would be ten years old then... 

SY: He would be 10 or 12. I think you were having your 12th 
birthday. 

TY: The reason I remember very vividly was because it was the 
last year the Maple Leafs won the Stanley Cup and, when 
we got to Hollyburn, which was not Hollyburn but the 
Tilley Estate we ... I was shuffled off upstairs with the 
caretaker to watch the playoffs with the Montreal 
Canadiens. Meanwhile, Dad took a walk around with the 
agent and was only gone one period (which was 20 minutes) 
and he said, “I am phoning home and...” 

SY: He phoned right away, and I will tell you what he said ... 
he said ... I lifted up the phone and he said, “I found it”. 
I said, “What are you talking about? Where are you ...” 
He said, “I have found it. I have found our Camp” . . . 
just like that. Now this was on a Monday, it was actually 
April the 29th which was his birthday but it was on a 
Monday and no maybe it was a weekend I don’t know what 
day it was, but he said, “I won’t be home for 2 or 3 days. 
I am going to see Ken Lemon and I want you to come down 
here on Saturday •. 

TY: I was really happy because I was missing school... 

SY: I went down on a Saturday and he had Sid Reynolds, who 
used to be one of his Section Directors, come up and meet 
him. We all met at Hollyburn and, in less than half an 
hour, I knew this was it. There was no question about it. 
That was in April and we moved from Sault St. Marie at 
the end of August because Ted had to start with Seneca 
College. He got the job there, by the way, and we moved 
lock, stock and barrel with our four children. Judy was 
going into grade 13 and on to University the next year; we 
had the three boys; we sold our house; and there was never 
any question that it wasn’t going to work. Never any 
question because we believed in it. Ted had ail those 
years of experience in it and it was what he wanted to do 
and, surprisingly, it was what I wanted to do. I never 
could have imagined doing anything else. 

CC: However, you had been quite a few years out of the main 
stream of camping... 

SY: Three and a half years... 

CC: Was there any worry about where the campers would 
come from ... 



Hoskoka, Ontario 



SY: Well, we had to make our name known again and this time 
for ourselves not just for the YMCA, so if you would like 
to know how we did it we went down to the Sportsmen’s 
Show which was a two-week business, then, and had our 
booth. We did this for three years and, the first year, we 
met enough people coming by that we knew just from 
camping, who didn’t know we were back in camping. 
And that was how we did it! 

CC: Those people told their friends and away it went. 

SY: And the friends, friends and friends... 

CC: I remember Ted saying he had made the decision that 
Hollyburn should remain a small Camp. 

SY: Well, up to this point Ted had had Pine Crest which was 
85 staff and 210 campers. That was the last year we were 
there and he had felt that he had become just an adminis¬ 
trator. He did know the kids because he had been there 18 
years which was a lot of continuity ... a rarity in the Y. 
I don’t think they have ever had it since. Camie Cameron 
ran Pine Crest for something like 12 years. When we first 
went, we thought we will never ever be there 12 years and 
here we achieved 18. We are almost 20 years at Hollyburn 
... I can’t believe that ... no wonder my hair is gray. 
Anyway,... 

TY: A lot of it goes back to the original camping. He wanted to 
get a lot of that same feeling of intimacy and be able to 
interact with the kids on a very personal basis, so he put 
everything into practice at Hollyburn that he felt to be 
ideal camping. 

SY: Well, a lot of people asked us why we were small and why 
we did this and why we did that. We would always say 
because all the years Ted was in camping he trialed and 
errored everything, and he wanted this to be more or less 
his ideal. But the reason it was a Boys’ and Girls’ Camp as 
against a Boys’ Camp (which he had always been involved 
in) was because of our daughter Judy and me. It was 
going to be a whole family thing and we both wanted to be 
in it with both feet. If it had just been a Boys’ Camp, it 
wouldn’t have been the same and another influence on 
that was the Family Y at Sault St. Marie. Ted was adamant 
about making the distinction between what was a co-ed 
camp and what was a Boys’ and Girls’ Camp. He felt that 
boys want to be boys and girls want to be girls, but the 
family idea, there would be enough mixing naturally in a 
Camp setting without calling it Co-ed. 

CC: Did you operate Hollyburn in the winter time right from 
the beginning? 

SY: I would say that grew like topsy. We knew that eventually 
we wanted to live there and, five years later, we built a 
home there. I suppose, in a sense, to justify living there, we 
wanted to do something with what we had. We would look 
around and see all these acres of land and just us enjoying 
it and we felt that other people should enjoy it. Partly 
from a financial point of view but also from a sociable 
point of view, we started with Hollyburn families and then 
from the Hollyburn families coming up as a group on one 
weekend, it grew just like topsy. It wasn’t originally in¬ 
tended but eventually became a sort of year-round 
operation. 

CC: And at the time, Ted was a teaching master at Seneca 
College... 

SY: For seven years. We built our home here five years later 
and, so that the boys could go to school, I stayed up here 
with them and Ted commuted every weekend. It was a 
double load in a sense ... 

CC: Boy, it sure was ... 

SY: But, for seven years, he did that just to be sure things 
would go ... 


CC: And did you keep the small numbers, were you able to 
maintain that... 

SY: Yes, we started with 55, then we went to 72, then we went 
to 84, then we went to 98 and that is the way it has always 
been. It was something that was a dream come true, it 
really was and it certainly was for Ted. We had always 
said, “Well, I guess we will not ever ...’’ Everybody has a 
dream and not everybody can realize it but it is good to 
have that goal. There we are with goals again . . . always 
reaching up for something. 

CC: Was he involved in the Camping Association in B.C. before 
he moved east? 

SY: No, I don't think so, not that I know of . . . was there a 
Camping Association then ... 

CC: Well, it was started just about the time he was getting into 
things, I have it in my records as 1937, but there are people 
in B.C. who tell me it was 1940 that the B.C. Association 
was officially begun. 

SY: As far as I know, Ted was not involved in the Camping 
Association in B.C. 

CC: But he was President of the Ontario Camping Association 
. . . and President of the Canadian Camping Association. 
Then, he came back for another tour of duty with the 
Ontario Association as Treasurer from 1971 - 1974. 

SY: I think he had something to do with Eanswythe Flynn and 
the editorial part of the Camping Association, did he not? 

CC: Yes, he did... 

SY: I think so because that was maybe his first love . . . 
writing. 

CC: We have just looked over past articles for the CANADIAN 
CAMPING MAGAZINE and he was by far the most 
prolific writer for the CANADIAN CAMPING 
MAGAZINE. Then, of course, when he was President of 
CCA, you had that cross-country trip where it started a 
whole lot of balls bouncing that had repercussions for 
many, many years to come. 

SY: Well, I think that Ted was in a way a pioneer with a lot 
of things, but then perhaps he lived in a time when there 
were pioneers, do you know what I mean... 

CC: And when pioneering was possible ... 

SY: Because now there aren’t so many things you can start in 
camping that are so significant. 

CC: That may be, but I think what makes a pioneer is someone 
who is reaching into new frontiers ... it takes a unique 
individual to be able to do that and Ted was that kind of 
person ... he was reaching out into new areas because he 
had the vision... 

TY: To see what was there and to make something out of it, 
I think that is the difference. 

CC: Certainly in all my years in YMCA camping and beyond, 
he was our dauntless leader and that pioneering spirit was 
probably what made him such a great man. If he was with 
us right now . . . and we were able to interview him . . . 
how do you suppose he would finish it off if I were to ask 
him... 

SY: Well, I think he would probably say he was a very fortunate 
person because few people realize their dreams and 
ambitions. As Ted once said to me, “Very few people do as 
much with their lives as Ted did and to influence so 
many...” 

CC: You mean your son, Ted, said that... 

SY: Yes, when sometimes I would feel that the best... some of 
the best . • • years of his life were . . • missed. But, few 
people realize their ambitions and few people pack so much 
into that short time... 


15 




TY: We often think he didn’t have time to enjoy it, to rest and 
look back on it, but he probably wouldn’t have rested and 
looked back anyway. I don’t think it would be possible for 
him to sit back and sort of watch someone else do it. 

CC: Was it ordained that Ted Jr. would eventually step into 
his father’s shoes ... 

TY: It would never be that anyway, and that is something I 
often have to deal with . . . people saying I look like him 
... I sound like him . . . but I know I am very different. 
What there is, though, is a common understanding now. 
It was never said, but I found, when I first directed Camp, 
I was trying to find explanations for things that people 
were asking me and I was doing it out of instinct. Now, I 
can rationalize things, explain things and understand about 
how we do things at Hollybum, because I have an under¬ 
standing of what T.Y. was all about, even though it was 
never really explained to me. Whether it was preordained 
that I do it, I don’t think so. I believe it was fate, because 
when Darlene and I came back from Vancouver with the 
idea of taking over, it was before we knew Dad was ill and 
it is difficult to say whether I could have done it knowing 
that he was ill. I know we came back because it was some¬ 
thing we wanted to do. 

SY: We have always felt that Ted and Darlene came to Holly- 
burn by choice... because we didn’t know. It was a matter 
of weeks until we discovered Ted was terminally HI. 

TY: It was within a few weeks though and that is very eerie 
because Dad was not the kind of person you could share a 
common position with. While we often saw the same end 
result, it wasn’t always the same route to get there. Dad

—-Ac.C.A./A.C.C. 50th Anniversary 

Patrons’ Fund 

“If you have built castles in the air, your work need not be lost; 
that is where they should be. Now, put foundations under them.” 

Henry David Thoreau 

In order to have something that is long lasting and enduring, it is essential to have a 
firm foundation. 

So it is with CCA /ACC. We need a solid foundation to assure its success, growth, 
development and impact. 

The kind of support CCA/ACC is seeking, right now, is financial. An additional 
income of $30,000.00, this year, represents the difference between a giant step forward 
and an irretrievable step backward. 

Can you help to propel us into overdrive? 

Our requirement of $30,000.00 is immediate. Our long-term goal is to establish a 
CCA/ACC Patrons’ Foundation whose proceeds will perpetuate camping in Canada. 
Automatically, by being a part of one, you become an important part of the other. 

You may donate any amount you wish. If we realize “thirty thou” in 1986, it will permit 
us some elbow room to build up our Patrons’ Foundation. 

We are sending this plea to approximately 100 people — some current Camp Directors, 
some retired Camp Directors, some friends of camping. The CCA/ACC’s Federal 
Charitable Number allows for substantial tax relief on all donations. 

If you know people associated with camping who might be interested in participating in 
this project but haven’t been contacted, please pass along their names to us. 

Surely this must be the most productive investment we can make in our lifetime — 
the future of camping. The returns are immediate. They multiply like crazy. There is no 
gamble involved, no speculation. 

In due course, we will send you a pledge card. At this time, our main purpose is to 
stimulate positive thinking about how we can assist in the growth of Canadian 
Camping. 

Most sincerely, 

Janet Adamson, Jack Pearse, 

President, Chairman, 

Canadian Camping Association. CCA/ACC Patrons’ Foundation.

SOME THOUGHTS FOR THE DAY 


A DIFFERENCE TO BE A DIFFERENCE HAS TO MAKE A 
DIFFERENCE. 

Gertrude Stein 


ALL THE FLOWERS OF TOMORROW ARE IN THE SEEDS 
OF TODAY. 

Plante M. Deep 

THE DESK MOTTO WE LIKE A LOT READS “RIGHT NOW 
IS A GOOD TIME.” 

Don D. Lay 

THE TROUBLE WITH NOT HAVING A GOAL IS THAT 
YOU CAN SPEND YOUR LIFE RUNNING UP AND DOWN 
THE FIELD AND NEVER SCORING. 

Bill Copeland 

IF YOU CAN’T BE BIG, DON’T BELITTLE. 

Hi Thaut 


THE ONLY PERSON WHO EVER GOT EVERYTHING 
DONE BY FRIDAY WAS ROBINSON CRUSOE. 

Ray Bowers 


EVEN A WOODPECKER OWES HIS SUCCESS TO THE 
FACT THAT HE USES HIS HEAD AND KEEPS PECKING 
AWAY UNTIL HE FINISHES THE JOB HE STARTS. 

Coleman Cox 


PASS IT ON 

Do you know a white oak leaf? — pass it on. 

Can you tie a bowline or a reef? — pass it on. 

Launch a rocket, do the “J”, 

If you are lost by night or day, 

And you know what to do —just pass it on. 

Can you lift a packsack? — pass it on. 

What about your super snack? — pass it on. 

If you have a swimming crest 
Or know the water safety test 
Then share the wealth with others — pass it on. 

When you ’re happy every day — pass it on. 

Wear a smile — Say “hokahay” — pass it on. 

Now you know that you belong 

Or if you have a brand new song 

It *s all the same, if you just — pass it on. 

You there with that hand to shake — pass it on. 

Even with the bread you bake — pass it on. 

Boiling up a cookout dog 
Or chopping through a stubborn log 
If you know how to do it — pass it on. 

Your pre-camp preparation — pass it on. 

With heartfelt dedication — pass it on. 

At camp’s the time for us to share 
And show our friends we really care 
So come on everybody — pass it on, pass it on, 
pass it on! 

by Jack Pearse 


A SMILE IS A CURVE THAT SETS THINGS STRAIGHT. 

Pearl E. Whyte 

THE KINDEST WORD IN ALL THE WORLD IS THE 
UNKIND WORD, UNSAID. 

Cille de Lipps 

“IT CAN BE DONE” IS GOOD; BUT “IT’S DONE” IS 
BETTER. 

B.L. Urt 


REMEMBER THE TEA KETTLE. THOUGH UP TO ITS 
NECK IN HOT WATER, IT CONTINUES TO SING. 

P. Coe 


A PAT ON THE BACK, ALTHOUGH ONLY A FEW 
VERTEBRAE REMOVED FROM A KICK IN THE PANTS, 
IS MILES AHEAD IN RESULTS. 

Bennett Cerf 

THE SMALLEST DEED IS BETTER THAN THE 
GRANDEST INTENTION. 

Larry Eisenberg 

ONE THING WE DO KNOW ABOUT THE SPEED OF 
LIGHT, IT GETS THERE TOO EARLY IN THE MORNING. 

Rhyse N. Bell 


TO A FRIEND 

You entered my life in a casual way, 

And saw at a glance what I needed; 

There were others who passed me or met me each day, 

But never a one of them heeded. 

Perhaps you were thinking of other folks more, 

Or chance simply seemed to decree it; 

I know there were many such chances before, 

But the others — well, they didn’t see it. 

You said just the thing that I wished you would say, 

And you made me believe that you meant it; 

I held up my head in the old gallant way, 

And resolved you should never repent it. 

There are times when encouragement means such a lot, 

And a word is enough to convey it; 

There were others who could have, as easy as not — 

But, just the same, they didn’t say it. 

There may have been someone who could have done more 
To help me along, though I doubt it; 

What I needed was cheering, and always before 

They had let me plod onward without it. 

You have helped to refashion the dream of my heart, 

And made me turn eagerly to it; 

There were others who might have (I question that part) — 
But, after all, they didn’t do it! 

by Grace Strieker Dawson 


17 




OUR PAL JOEY 


A True Story Of A Camping Crow 
by TED YARD 

Director YMCA Camp Pine Crest 





This article is reprinted from Canadian 
Camping Magazine, Dec. 1962. 

Notre Ami Joey 

Voici I’histoire vraie d’une corneille 
campeuse; un joli recit d’une amiti6 
que se forme entre un animal de la 
foret, le chien du directeur et une 
multitude de campeurs. 

It’s over a year since Joey first arrived 
at Pine Crest, and started his career as pet 
and entertainer at this YMCA boys* 
summer camp. Since last summer 
however, the great uncertainty about his 
whereabouts and health — if indeed he 
was still alive — had always deterred us 
from telling his story. 

Joey was just a little crow when a 
camper’s parent first brought him to us. 
Unable to fend for himself, he found 
plenty of young friends to pop tasty 
morsels into the gaping beak that seemed 
to hold out a tin cup on many a cabin 
porch rail. Joey thrived on attention and 
good food, and in no time flew capably 
about the Camp on his daily “scrounging 
missions”, making friends wherever he 
went. 

Among Joey’s friends were two who 
figure largely in the story of his stay with 
us. Sid, the Director of the Junior Boys 
Section was one of these. Joey would 
perch on Sid’s hat or on his shoulder and 
even pick bread out of his benefactor’s 


shirt pocket. Occasionally he’d grab one 
of the cigars that were ever present in this 
pocket and carry it off triumphantly to a 
secret hiding place. Sid was very thought¬ 
ful of his new-found friend. A dish of 
water on the porch rail, and a genuine 
love for each living creature helped to 
provide the bond between bird and man. 
If they didn’t speak the same language 
they certainly seemed to understand one 
another remarkably well! Sitting on Sid’s 
hat, Joey “mugged” his way into a CBC 
camping film shown on the Trans- 
Canada television network — Joey 
seemed destined for fame! 

Soon he found another playmate; one 
whom he could pester and tease; one who 
never tired of chasing after him, and one 
who would never be smart enough to 
catch him. This was “Buzzy”, the Camp 
Director’s dog. “Buzzy” has a somewhat 
obscure origin, but he’s called an 
“Eskimo hunting dog” which seems to 
cover most possibilities! Buzz is as white 
as Joey is black, and early in the season 
his main exercise came from countless 
futile sorties after scurrying chipmunks 
and squirrels. Then Joey came along! 

Each morning Joe would be waiting for 
Buzz to come out of the cottage. With a 
crackling squawk he’d flutter to the 
ground dragging a supposedly broken 
wing, and when the pup bounded after 
him, Joe would take off, flying low over 
Buzzy’s head and laughing his most 
taunting laugh! Buzz would take up the 
chase, usually oblivious to where Joe was 
leading him, and on more than one 
occasion the wiley low-flying joker took 
him right off the dock into the lake! 
Several times Joe tried to lead his play¬ 
mate over a high rock ledge, but always 
the pup sensed the danger just in time. 

All-in-all the crow had a hilarious 
time! On the football field he would strut 
around pecking at the soccer ball and 
acting like an international centre 
forward — until Buzz arrived to send him 
“to the showers”. 

When Camp closed last year the crow 
missed the children’s attention and 
decided to concentrate on tormenting 
Buzzy. One evening, just before Labour 
Day, he’d been up to his old tricks. 
Swooping low through a stand of 
hemlocks he laughed hilariously at the 
pup whom he had again so easily out¬ 
witted. But his laugh trailed off into a wild 


cackle as he banged squarely into one of 
the trees and fell to the ground! Buzzy ran 
right over him and was several yards past 
before he could pull up to a stop. By this 
time Joey had struggled up and lumbered 
over to a bridge rail where he sulkily 
surveyed the site of his near demise. That 
dejected picture was our last glimpse of 
him. Was he hurt badly? Did a hawk get 
him? Did he go south? We often 
wondered. 


This season many campers have asked 
about Joey. While we had little hope, we 
really didn’t know what had happened to 
him, so we always said, “probably some 
day he will be back again.” 

At noon on August 16, Sid came into 
the dining hall looking something like a 
bishop who had just won a raffle. A 
rumor rumbled around tables lighting up 
the faces of all who heard it. Then a black 
shadow swooped by the front of the 
building. There on his old ledge was our 
pal Joey! 

During the winter he had acquired a 
new cry strangely like that of a child 
calling “mama”, and now he picked up 
right where he had left off with the 
campers and with the pup. 

To-night as I write this, Joey is crest¬ 
fallen! Three wing feathers on the ground 
bear mute evidence to his latest brash 
escapade. During the supper hour he had 
perched in a tree by the dining hall 
apparently enjoying one of our ten- 
minute Muskoka showers. Then, forgett¬ 
ing that his wings were wet, he dropped 
down to tease the pup again. Buzzy 
caught his tormentor and gathered in 
three black chevrons. Joey, his pride 
sorely wounded, fled to a nearby tree 
scolding profanely. This is a little reminis¬ 
cent of last season’s end. But we hope, 
somehow, that this season the trickster 
will be a better sport, swallow his pride, 
and stay around camp, oh — quite a bit 
longer! 



‘T. Y. and two boys puzzle through a model 
compass together”

AN EXPERIENCE AT * w 
THE Y.M.C.A. 

UNITED NATIONS SEMINAR 


Les Nations • Unies 

Alors que Ted Yard §tait Secretaire 
du YMCA, il a eu I’occasion de visiter 
les Nations-Unies. It a 6t6 invite k se 
presenter kune salle sp£ciale portant 
I’inscription: “Cette salle est d6diee k 
la Paix et a tous ceux qui travaiilent 
en son nom c'est une piece ou le 
silence est de mise et ou seul les 
pensees ont droit de parole.” 

Cet episode dans cette piece a 
inspire Ted k faire des reflections sur 
le but de sa mession avec le YMCA et 
le Camping, Ses pensees nous 
encouragent tous k faire de m§me 
face k nos responsabilites en tant que 
leaders de lajeunesse. 

Several years ago, I was privileged 
to be among the thirty-one secretaries 
from Canada and the United States, 
attending a Seminar on the United 
Nations at U.N. Headquarters. During 
our Seminar week we had opportunities to 
visit many areas; the General Assembly, 
the Security Council, as well as other 
councils and committees. There were 
briefing sessions, when we learned about 
the workings of the world organization; 
visits to missions from several countries 
when we were able to ask the questions 
which were uppermost in our minds; even 
planned meal-time discussions with 
“U.N. Fellows” from countries around 
the globe. 

Meetings were held at various offices 
and embassies, but the focal point was 
the strikingly designed United Nations on 
the East River. Upon entering the main 
hallway of this building, one has a feeling 
of standing at a great crossroads of 
the world. Across this amazingly quiet, 
75 foot high hall, thousands of persons 
pass each day .... persons of every 
colour and race; persons from a hundred 
countries; persons ranging in age from 
the many classes of visiting school 
children to the elder statesmen of the 
world. Over to the right, off the beaten 
track, and away from the hurly-burly an 
alcove ... a low railing; a carpeted floor; 
a guest bench, and dedication plaque, 
convey the message — “this is a place of 
quiet”. Beside a door which leads to a 
dark passageway and a small room, a 
plaque carries the following inscription: 

4 This is a room devoted to peace and to 
those who are giving themselves for peace . 
It is a room of quiet where only thoughts 
shall speak". 

We were interested in all this, and 
stepped in quietly, groping our way at first 
until our eyes became adjusted to the dim 


light... then we sat for a moment on the 
simple cane benches at one end of the 
small room. One shaft of light from the 
ceiling shining on a large block of iron ore 
in the center of the room, was the only 
source of illumination. 

The meaning of this place is perhaps 
best conveyed in the words of Dag 
Hammarskjold, the late Secretary 
General, as he dedicated the room. 

€t We all have within us a center of 
stillness surrounded by silence. 

This house , dedicated to work and 
debate in the service of peace, should have 
one room dedicated to silence in the 
outward sense and stillness in the inner 
sense. 

It has been the aim to create in this 
small room a place where the doors may 
be open to the infinite lands of thought 
and prayer. 

People of many faiths will meet here, 
and for that reason none of the symbols to 
which we are accustomed in our 
meditation could be used. 

However, there are simple things which 
speak to us all with the same language. 
We have sought for such things and we 
have found them in the shaft of light 
striking the shimmering surface of solid 
rock. 

So, in the middle of the room we see a 
symbol of how, daily, the light of the skies 
gives life to the earth on which we stand, a 
symbol to many of us of how the light of 
the spirit gives light to the matter. 

But the stone in the middle of the room 
has more to tell us. We may see it as an 
altar, empty not because there is no God, 
not because it is dedicated to the God 
whom man worships under many names 
and in many forms. 

The stone in the middle of the room 
reminds us also of the firm and permanent 
in a world of movement and change. The 
block of iron ore has the weight and 
solidity of the everlasting. It is a reminder 
of that comer stone of endurance and 
faith on which all human endeavour must 
be based. 

The material of the stone leads our 
thoughts to the necessity for choice 
between destruction and construction, 
between war and peace. Of iron man has 
forged his swords, of iron he has also 
made his ploughshares. Of iron he has 
constructed tanks, but of iron he has 
likewise built homes for man. The block 
of iron ore is part of the wealth we have 
inherited on this earth of ours. How are 
we to use it? 

The shaft of light strikes the stone in a 


room of utter simplicity. There are no 
other symbols, there is nothing to distract 
our attention or to break in on the stillness 
within ourselves. When our eyes travel 
from these symbols to the front wall, they 
meet a simple pattern opening up the 
room to the harmony, freedom and 
balance of space. 

There is an ancient saying that the sense 
of a vessel is not in its shell but in the void. 
So it is with this room. It is for those who 
come here to fill the void with what they 
find in their center of stillness, ” 

We were sitting only a minute when a 
loud noise shattered the peace of the 
place. A large woman came bustling in, 
then stumbled over one of the benches, 
cursed the whole place as a “deathtrap” 
and shouted for someone to “get me out 
of here.” An efficient guard seemed to 
appear from nowhere and politely helped 
the poor woman out to the lobby. As she 
went she swore that this would be 
reported to the 125,000 women of 
America whom she represented . . . and 
then all was quiet again. 

Somehow it was all so incongrous, and 
yet so completely relative to the problems 
that face this great agent for world peace. 
Ignorance — the ignorance that would 
exclude any sensitivity for the carefully 
prepared entrance to a place of quiet; 
ignorance that must surely be the 
greatest single obstacle to mutual 
understanding. 

Fear — the fear of the dark, leading to 
panic and unrestrained irresponsible 
conduct. Fear, warping the conduct of 
the littlest child and of the greatest 
nation. 

Fear the handmaid of ignorance in a 
world where the need for greater 
knowledge and for trust becomes ever 
more apparent and where neither East 
nor West, white or black, yellow or 
brown can be cast in the role of teacher 
or student. Strangely perhaps, no one 
has a monopoly on the ignorance, the 
fear, the knowledge or the faith. 

We were impressed with the unpar¬ 
allelled opportunities for service open to 
our own association, both at home and 
abroad. Opportunities in our youth 
programs, in physical education, in 
camping, in fact wherever we meet with 
people in purposeful program situations. 

We were indeed moved to hope and 
pray that we and our colleagues will be 
given the strength to pause as individuals 
and as an association for periods of 
mediation and quiet, that we may indeed 
be refreshed, rededicated, and enabled to 
see ever more clearly the Young Men’s 
Christian Association’s great challenge 
. . . “that they all may be one”. May we 
recognize in our Christian heritage the 
stuff to fill many a void in human 
experience and may we constantly seek 
further opportunities to accomplish this.

THE DUKE OF EDINBURGH’S 
AWARD IN CANADA 

A Challenge To Camp Directors Across Canada 



Through Camp Directors, campers and staff in Canadian 
Camps are encouraged to seriously investigate the possibilities of 
becoming involved in one of the most prestigious achievement 
award programs for young people between the ages of 14 - 25. As 
a result of the regular programs which already exist in most 
Canadian Camps, the opportunity becomes a very obvious one. 

At this time, there are already 40,000 Canadians partici¬ 
pating in the Duke of Edinburgh’s Award program, either as 
members of organized groups such as guiding, scouting, cadets, 
church and schools. But Camps have not yet realized the full 
potential of the advantages of the program. Camps are a 
“natural”, and the prestige of having some of the young people 
from our camps receive the Bronze, Silver or Gold Award is 
something which should be given serious consideration — and 
even begin this summer. 

Participation in the Award Program represents a personal 
commitment to constructive endeavour, promoting qualities of 
self-discipline, self-help and self-reliance ... surely the qualities 
which we in camping so heartily espouse. 

There are three levels — Bronze, Silver and Gold. Within each 
level, there are four categories, the terms of which can be 
achieved over whatever period of time the candidate chooses. 
BUT MANY OF THE CONDITIONS CAN BE STARTED AND 
CONTINUED AT A SUMMER CAMP. Initially, the candidate 
either on his or her own (or through the Camp Director) obtains a 
record book. And then one level at a time can be obtained by each 
participant. 

The National Office address is: 203 - 86 Overlea Blvd. 

Toronto, Ontario 
M4H 1C6 
(416) 429-1200 

There are Regional offices in each Province. 


The Chairman of the Awards Program is The Right 
Honourable Jeanne Sauve, Governor General of Canada, and the 
Patron is of course, His Royal Highness Prince Philip, Duke of 
Edinburgh. 

Every Camp Director across Canada is urged to look seriously 
at this exciting, worthwhile program. And it goes without saying 
that your campers who become involved will always feel proud of 
their accomplishment and achievement — made even more 
significant by knowing that they began the program at Camp.
