“OUR FRAGILE WORLD - 
A CHALLENGE FOR THE 
OUTDOOR COMMUNITY” 


SECOND INTERNATIONAL CAMPING CONGRESS 

March 3-5,1987 Shoreham Hotel Washington, D.C. 


*Jointly Sponsored by 
the American Camping Association 
the Canadian Camping Association 
the Jamaica Camping and Hiking Association 
the National Camping Association of Japan 

Purpose 

The Second International Camping Congress is an event to bring together the practitioners of the 
outdoor experience movement from many nations and related organizations to examine the 
elements of our fragile world which challenge the organized camping, environmental, and 
experiential education community to impact participants for future action. 



The Congress is Calling Canadians! 

There are special rates, special air fares, special alternate accommodations and special Canadian events. Canadians are making major 
contributions: You can expect to see Dorothy Walter, Jack Pearse, Fred Okada, Jocelyn Palm and Rob Heming as just part of our 
Congress commitment. Canadians can also bring home valuable camping advice in many interests areas: public relations, personnel, 
leadership, support services, business, finances, marketing, and program. 



Glen Bernard Camp

UNDER OPEN SKIES 
A ciel ouvert 

Le 15 janvier 1983, un service commemoratif pour Ted 
Yard a eu lieu au Camp Hollyburn a Rosseau, Ont. On y a lu 
le poeme qui suit. 

Un po6me eloqieux k la mesure de I’homme qu’il etait. 

On Jan. 15, 1983, a memorial service for Ted Yard was held at 
Camp Hollyburn, Rosseau, Ontario. This poem was read: 

BRIDGE BUILDER 

An old man, going a lone highway 
Came at the evening, cold and gray 
To a chasm, vast and deep and wide, 

Through which was flowing a sullen tide. 

The old man crossed in the twilight dim, 

The sullen stream had no fears for him. 

But he paused when safe on the other side 
And built a bridge to span the tide. 

“Old man ”, said a fellow pilgrim near, 

”You are wasting strength with building here; 

Your journey will end with the ending day, 

And you never again will pass this way. 

You have crossed this chasm deep and wide, 

Why build you the bridge at the eventide?” 

The builder lifted his old grey head — 

“Good friend, in the path I have come, ” he said, 

“There follows after me today 
A youth whose feet must pass this way. 

This chasm that has been nothing to me 
To that fair-haired youth may a pitfall be; 

He, too, must cross in the twilight dim, 

Good friend, I am building that bridge for him . " 

What a fitting tribute to a great man. 

AN IRISH BLESSING 

from the Gaelic 
May the blessing of LIGHT be on you, 

Light without, and light within. 

May the blessed sunlight shine on you 
And warm your heart, till it glows like a great peat fire 
So that the stranger may come and warm himself at it — 
and also a friend 

May the light shine out of the two eyes of you like candles 
Set in the windows of a house, 

Bidding the wanderer to come in out of the storm. 

And may the blessing of the RAIN be on you — 
the soft sweet rain. 

May it fall upon your spirit so that all the flowers may i 
spring up and shed their sweetness on the air; 

And may the blessing of the great RAINS be on you: 

May they beat upon your spirit and wash it fair and clean, 
And leave a shining pool where the blue of heaven shines * 
in it — and sometimes a star. 

And may the blessings of the EARTH be upon you — 
the great round earth; 

May you ever have a kindly greeting for those who 
pass as you are going along its roads. 

May the earth be soft under you when you lie upon it, 
tired, at the end of the day. 

And may it rest easy over you when at last you lie down 
under it; 

May it rest so lightly over you that your soul may 
be quickly through it 
And up and off on its way to God. 

So might it be. 


A Counsellor's Prayer 

Put me in touch with the heart of the child, 

Let me study his doubts and fears; 

Let me try to show him the way of life 
And help him avoid its tears: 

For the heart of a child in its bouyancy 
Is one that is pure and free. 

So put me in touch with the heart of a child 
Of the Person — that-is-to-be! 

C. Burt is Hunter

The Onondaga presented the Seneca with 
a Table. 

We the people of the Onondaga tribe 
offer this table to you the people of the 
Seneca tribe. It is bonded together with 
great strength just as we the people are 
bonded with the great strength of friend¬ 
ship. 

The Cayuga presented the Onondaga with 
a Bear’s Paw. 

The Bear Paw made as a gift to the 
Onondaga tribe is meant to symbolize the 
forging of the elements of the earth: 

The Bear Paw and the leather used as a 
base represent the living or animal part of 
the world. The bark represents the 
necessity of plant life to the existence of 
the living earth. The shells represent the 
sea or the water and its role as an integral 
pan of this earth. The feathers represent 
the Sun and the Sky as well as the Air we 
breathe. The blending of all the elements 
also symbolizes the need for all people to 
live and work together in peace and order 


for the world to survive. If even one 
element is missing the balance becomes 
upset. 

The Tuscarora gave the Oneida a 
Tomahawk. 

We, the people of the Tuscarora, offer 
this Tomahawk to our brothers the 
Oneida, as a token of our friendship and a 
symbol of the lasting peace between the 
tribes. May it bring you good luck in your 
hunting for many moons to come. 

The Oneida presented the Cayuga with a 
Mystic Rock! 

We the Oneida tribe present this Mystic 
Rock as a gift of friendship, love and 
peace to you, the Cayuga. This token 
represents the goodness and forgiveness 
that we each possess, so that we may live 
together as one: with trust, peace, love, 
and friendship throughout the coming 
ages! 

The Mohawks presented the Tuscarora 
with a Worldly Stone. 


We the Mohawks give the people of 
Tuscarora the Worldly Stone as a peace 
offering and a symbol of our tribe. 

Red represents fire — to give you warmth 
White represents clouds — to give you 
rain 

Black — to remind you of evil storms 
Blue — for water to give you great crops 

Please take this offering as a symbol of 
peace and friendship between our tribes. 

COUNCIL CLOSING 

May the Peace of the Forest, 

The Song of the Birds, 

The Inspiration of the Hills, 

The Warmth of the Sun, 

The Strength of the Trees, 

The Fragrance of the Flowers, 

The Joy of the Wind, 

The Calm of the Lake, 

In All of Which is the Creator of Good 
Things be in Your Hearts Tonight and 
Always. 


PROGRAMS AT CAMP 

by Liz Greenway — Central Region Editor 

Who plans the programs at your camp — staff or campers? 
What about the big day — the regatta, the all camp program, the 
special event, the extravaganza, the things campers remember and 
that exhaust staff? Does a small group of campers or staff plan 
your big day, spending hours getting props together, making signs 
or decorations, planning all the details? 

There is another way. This is where the preparation is the 
program. Consider a football game, the Royal Wedding, a 
Cabaret, a Superstars Competition. 

In this instance everyone has a part to play. A football game 
(or a baseball game) — where one group is the half-time show, 
another group the cheerleaders with practical routines, a medical 
crew with tent, stretchers and intravenous, a refreshment crew 
who have made the popcorn and drinks, costumes, and boxes to 
carry refreshments, a security group who have made tickets and 
sold them for a song to escort dignitaries, a facility crew in charge 
of lining the Field, setting up bleachers, scoreboards and physical 
arrangements, a group in charge of opening ceremonies, 
dignitaries and post game presentation, a group of officials and 
oh yes let’s not forget the game itself! The creativity is always 
exciting as each group thinks of more and more things they can do 
to make it an event. 

The campers who do 90% of the physical work itself, always have 
a million ideas and require staff as consultants but are delighted 
with the results they have achieved. 

This type of program is not the answer to every program but we 
should provide the opportunity for everyone to plan, for everyone 
to be the program. 

If you have a program idea or comments on programs why not 
share it with others. Send the information to Liz Greenway 
c/o C.C.A. office. 



“Northern Saskatchewan Twilight.” Camp Christopher N. of Prince 
Albert, Sask. 


j- 


25 





SELLING YOUR CAMP PROGRAM 

by Ian Fowler 

Outdoor Recreation Co-ordinator 
City of Moncton 

The aspect of promotion and public relations is a key ingredient 
to the success of any business and those of us in the camping 
industry are not exempt from selling ourselves if we wish to be 
successful in attracting new campers and maintaining those we 
currently have. 

To me, the difficulty in assessing your camp’s promotion/ 
public relations is where to begin. In talking with fellow Camp 
Directors, it is very apparent the differences in the styles of camp 
promotion/public relations programs are as varied as the 
individual camps. With everything from color glossy brochures, 
to sophisticated pre-camp packages, to photocopied camp flyers, 
the Camp Director assessing a promotion/public relations 
program has endless questions to address. 

In developing such a program for our camp within the City of 
Moncton, I was faced with these questions. 

My first question, however, was not should we have a 
promotion/public relations package, but do we have a quality 
product worthy of promotion? I believe that, if you cannot 
answer this question in a positive manner, then perhaps time 
should be spent on program development rather than public 
relations. 

Far too often, we take the “cart before the horse” philosophy 
having all the bells and whistles for a successful promotion/ 
public relations campaign, only to find our product, in this case 
the camp program, is not at the level it should be, resulting in 
negative promotion from our clients. Certainly, our cheapest and 
most effective public relations tool is “word-of-mouth” 
promotion from our current campers and parents. My first 
suggestion, then, is to build a quality program before launching a 
major promotion/public relations campaign. Utilize “word-of- 
mouth” promotions to your advantage. 

The second aspect in developing your campaign is to select your 
target group. Not one of our camps can be everything to 
everyone, so be selective. Do you concentrate on single family 
campers? Campers from upper income families? Does your camp 
have a specific focal area such as sports? Know your knitting — 
select your target groups at which you wish to address your 
attention. 

Once the first two steps are completed, you are ready to 
develop an “Action Plan” for your camp promotion/public 
relations campaign. In developing this plan consider the 
following: 

— “Rome wasn’t built in a day” — You won’t be able to imple¬ 
ment everything in year one. Spread out your items in a 
realistic plan. 

— Look for high profile /low costs items, in the beginning, 
working your way along to the items with higher price tags. 

— Gauge yourself on spending approximately 3°/o of your total 
operating budget on promotions. 

To get you started with your plan, here are some specific 
suggestions that you may wish to use. 

PROMOTIONS: 

Media — Radio — public service announcements, talk shows, 
paid advertising. 

Television — public service announcements, talk 
shows, paid advertising, community 
T.V. shows. 

Newspaper — feature articles, paid advertising. 


PUBLIC RELATIONS: 

The public relations items listed are designed to let your campers 
and staff know you are thinking about them and keep them 
thinking about camp. These items traditionally cost more; 
however, the investment is well worth it. 

— Christmas letter or card to all campers/staff. 

— Section newsletter periodically throughout the year talking 
about what’s new at camp, general information, etc. 

— Camper reunions. 

— Registration package full of details needed upon registration. 

— Birthday card sent to all campers/staff. 

— Letters to parents from counsellor during or after camp 
session. 

Finally, there are four basic premises that I believe must be 
considered in the development of promotional and public relation 
items. 

1. We are professionals in the camping field . . . make sure all 
materials present a professional image. 

2. Be consistent with use of colour, logo, theme in all pro¬ 
motional material. 

3. Campaign must be ongoing and progressive. 

4. Continue to develop new ideas. 

Promotions and public relations can be an exciting area of 
challenge to all Camp Directors. Although it does require an 
investment of time and dollars, the rewards you will reap from 
developing a positive image will be worth the effort. 

And remember — Professionalism can be obtained at minimal 
cost. 

Special Flyers — Many communities have special supplements 
delivered weekly to homes in the community, 
often times providing free coverage to 
organizations. Specifically items such as — 
Real Estate Guide, Community T.V. Guide, 
Auto-Trader, (etc.) 

Public Speaking—Select groups which meet your target area. 

Suggestions include Home and School 
Associations, Service Clubs, Church Groups, 
Community Organizations, (etc.) 

Displays — Set up staffed camp displays at local trade shows 
or malls. 

Brochure— Your camp brochure is a valuable promotional tool. 

Develop a network list for distribution and keep tabs 
at what areas camper applications are obtained from. 

Open House — An opportunity to show off what you are all 
about. 

Many of the promotional items listed above cost 
nothing more than your time. As well, consult 
local cable T.V. stations, radio stations, and 
A.V. departments from local universities and 
community colleges. Quite often, these 
people are willing to volunteer their time to 
assist in developing promotional aids.

SUBSCRIPTION INFORMATION 

Canadian Camping Magazine is the official publication of the Canadian Camping Association. 
Editorial offices of the Magazine are located at R.R. HI, Huntsville, Ontario, P0A 1K0. 

Membership in the C.C.A., as a result of membership in a provincial camping association, 
includes a subscription to the Magazine. Non member subscription is S8.00/year. Single issue price 
is $2.00. Make cheques payable to the Canadian Camping Association. Send subscriptions, sub¬ 
missions, or address changes to the editorial offices. 

Canadian Camping Magazine is published four times yearly. Deadlines for submissions are 
October 1, December 1, February 15 and May 1. Material in Canadian Camping Magazine may 
not be reproduced in any form without the expressed written permission of the editor. Copyright 
1986 Canadian Camping Association.
